# 17-expanse — sources

P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's

post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.
- Tobias Brandt → [HN] the genomics comment (bursty pipeline, "about 8 different steps", "We need to reserve the $MAX requirements for each").
- Ana Lucía Ferreira → [HN] the student's "so I overestimate" on simulation time; the queue wait for a big request is the author's.
- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: It moves from where I sell, to the context, to my beliefs about the problem, to how interviews are run, and that matches how I'd explain Expanse, with the recency question on screen 4 only a brief detour inside the context step.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 show the same question, 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'; screens 8 and 9 look similar but are different questions (how many researchers vs. how many days).
founder.missing: The flow never asks who pays: my users are researchers, but my buyer is the cluster operator, paying per cluster, with a department running the pilot. It also never asks what Expanse does (an agent on every node predicting job sizes at submit time), my price and offer (a free two-week measurement, then a paid pilot at a fixed monthly fee), or the size of the waste as a share of the cluster's GPU hours, which is the cost my pitch rests on. Those operators can't be reached through a researcher-only link, so screen 16 doesn't cover them.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screening, then failure frequency, flows sensibly, but asking how sizing went on my last submission comes after the question about what I'd want made easier, when it should come first because submission happens before the failure and the choice is better informed by having walked through it.
PRIMARY.missing: Why the job failed (out of memory, hit the time limit, or something else), how much work was lost, and how much memory, GPU and run time I requested versus what the job actually used.

screens.why5: It keeps my word 'researchers' and changes nothing of what I typed about the job, the cluster or the guess.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, how researchers answer is the obvious next decision.
screens.why2: The choice is clear to me, but the "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" status and the "Hear her" link sit run together with the description and take a second read to separate.
screens.why3: I know how my researchers work, often at a desk in a shared lab or office, and whether they would rather read and tap than talk to a video interviewer.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete, and no escape chip is needed, but "Let them choose" hangs on "Ready when Daphne is", which leaves me working out how long it means and whether it holds up my send.
screens.why5: My researchers and the study are kept as I typed them, and nothing on this screen changes what my idea means.

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, the last step before sending is deciding who receives a link, so the question is obvious here.
screens.why2: The question and options are short and I can answer on first read; only 'the Contacts page' assumes a part of Keel I have not seen, and its option explains itself as a search.
screens.why3: I know how I would reach researchers: by name through the clusters and HPC contacts we already talk to, or by posting one link in a place like our HN thread or a cluster's Slack.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search list and one open link for a group are distinct, cover the ways I would reach researchers, and each says what happens to the link; no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The screen does not restate or alter my idea, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as typed.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits at the top with its deciding number beside it (Frequency: 4 answered), and the card adds that 5 are needed, so I know the problem is not called yet and why.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but the tally and card lines show the counts and bars; I need a second look to see why only 4 of the 7 who answered count on three cards, and how 'at least 8 in 10' becomes a bar of 6 of 7.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are the lines I checked, word for word, but Prevalence and Frequency narrow my problem to jobs failing partway, when my claim is as much about over-requesting and wasted compute.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the page never says so, nor who to ask, why 3 people dropped out, or what this means for the idea so far.
screens.why_b5: The counts are honest (n stays visible, 6 of 7 is only 'at the bar', low n is called too few), but my unproven statement that 'everyone over-requests' and most compute is wasted sits unlabelled under the verdict and could read as a finding.
screens.instead: Not called yet: 6 of 7 had a job fail partway, right at the bar, but only 4 of the 7 could answer the next three questions because the others did not qualify for them; get at least one more qualifying researcher before reading these as a result, and treat the statement above as my belief, not a finding.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar", so I get the verdict and the deciding number together, and they agree.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven cells, six for me and one against, with the marker at 6, and the question above it makes plain that it counts people who had a job fail partway through.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the name and mid-run failure as my problem, but my claim was that everyone over-requests to avoid failure, so "8 in 10 had a job fail partway through in 5 working days" is a narrower, reworded belief.
screens.why_b4: "How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards" tells me where to read next and not to lean on this alone, but not what this result means for the idea or what to do about it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the claim is limited to "these 7", the bar is called "exactly" met, and "a lean, not a call" says the group is too small to carry more.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only just: 6 of these 7 had a job fail partway through and one more no would drop it below your bar, so treat this as a lean and let the Frequency and Importance cards decide whether to keep building on failed jobs.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits directly beside the deciding number, 5 needed to call it and only 4 in, and the So line repeats it, although "4 answered" there really means 4 counted.
screens.why_b2: The axis and median show at once what is counted, but where the bar sits takes a second look: it reads "3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3)" while the strip has five cells and nothing states that all 4 landed inside my range.
screens.why_b3: Frequency and 3 to 5 working days out of 5 are the belief I checked, and the job failing partway through is my own words for the pain.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" tells me not to act on this and implies I am one counted answer short, but it never says to get that answer or what it would mean for the idea.
screens.why_b5: The n and small group are plain and nothing is called held, but the verdict's "4 answered" conflicts with the count line's "6 answered", and "a lean" sits awkwardly beside "nothing is settled".
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 people counted fall inside your 3 to 5 days, but you need 5 counted, and 2 of the 6 who answered could not be counted, so get one more researcher's clear answer before relying on this.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside the number that decides it, 4 against the 5 needed, and the So line repeats it.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the caption (4 people, 8 picks) read at once, but the bar is 3 of 4 people while the strip under it has 8 cells of picks with the marker at 3, so I had to look twice to see that the 3 for me are people and the 5 against are other picks.
screens.why_b3: The name, the belief line and "Guessing memory, GPUs and run time" are exactly what I checked on the way in, and the bar is the at least 2 in 3 I accepted.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing settled here yet" is honest, but it doesn't tell me that one more counted researcher would allow a call, or to get that answer before changing anything.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond these people and says plainly that a small group is a lean, not a call, but the headline's "4 answered" contradicts the count line's "6 answered · 4 counted".
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 researchers counted put guessing sizes in their top two, which is at the bar, but I need 5 counted (6 answered, 2 not counted), so get one more usable answer before treating this as settled.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" is plain and 5 needed is beside it, but the headline's "4 answered" disagrees with the count line's "6 answered · 4 counted", so the deciding number needs reconciling.
screens.why_b2: The groups, the line and who counts read quickly, but "your bar · 3 of 4" looks like my result rather than the bar, and I have to work out that the ghost cell is the one missing person.
screens.why_b3: The name, the belief line and the 2-in-3 bar against "Padded it a little" are the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is true but generic: it doesn't say I need one more countable answer, or what that means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim beyond the people who answered: n stays visible, the two uncounted people are named with reasons, and the small group is called a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 answered, 4 counted, 5 needed. 3 of the 4 fell short, which leans your way; get one more clear answer about a real last submission before you rely on it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly beside the number that decides it, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know where the line stands and why.
screens.why_b3: The name Importance and the belief line are word for word the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the screen never says so, and it does not say what Kwabena's answer means for the idea, such as checking whether data movement and software setup outrank sizing for teams that already size from past runs.
screens.why_b5: The screen makes no claim beyond its people: the status stays 'Too few to call', the counts are visible, and the single quote is labelled '1 against · 1 asked' and 'On their own (1)' rather than dressed up as a theme.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's quote adds something I did not type: someone whose sizes from last week's runs are fine loses the day to data movement and library conflicts, which are named rivals to my problem, though this is only one person.
screens.instead: Add after the quote: 'One person so far: their sizes from past runs are good enough, and data and software setup cost them more. Get more answers before calling this, and watch whether others on repeat workloads say the same.'

screens.why1: As the first screen of a study about cluster work, it makes obvious sense to check that I actually run jobs on a cluster of that size.
screens.why2: "Run jobs", "cluster" and "GPUs" are how I talk every day, and I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know the size of the cluster I submit to and whether I run jobs on it, though a shared or multi-partition setup might take a moment's thought.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for a screener, and the guidelines give a gate no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of clusters of 100 or more GPUs and shows nothing of a product, company or role label.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says cleanly aloud, and the only slight stiffness is "I'll read 2 options" before a plain yes or no.

screens.why1: After checking that I run on a cluster this size, it makes sense to ask whether I recently had a job die mid-run, and that sets up the story they ask for next.
screens.why2: "Job" and "fail partway through" are how I talk, and I can answer straight away, though I'd take a job killed for hitting its memory or time limit as a failure without being told.
screens.why3: I know whether one of my own jobs died this week from my scheduler logs and my own memory.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct, but two escapes is one too many, and "I can't recall one particular job submission" is an odd reply to a yes-or-no about any job failing.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks to me, but the founder's moment is having to guess memory, GPUs and run time before submitting, and this narrows it to jobs that failed, with no link to a bad guess, and the follow-up's "last job submission" may not even be the failed job.
screens.why6: It is one short question ending in "Yes or no", so I can hear it once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you have a job fail partway through? Yes / No, with no escape chip; on a yes, ask "Think of the last job that failed. Tell us what happened."

screens.why1: I just said yes to having a job fail in the last 5 working days, so asking how many days that happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Job failing partway through is exactly how I'd say it, and counting days in a work week needs no second read.
screens.why3: I know which days this week a run died from my scheduler emails and logs, so I can answer from what actually happened.
screens.why4: One to five covers every possible answer after a yes on the screen before, the numbers don't overlap, and I can't recall fits if the week is a blur.
screens.why5: Nothing of any product or founder language reaches me, and it still means a job failing during the window given.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and five single numbers plus one escape are easy to hold when heard once, though repeating the window from the last screen is slightly more than needed.

screens.why1: After asking how often my jobs died partway through, it makes sense to ask which part of running jobs bothers me most, and the anchor brings me back to my last run.
screens.why2: Allocation, memory, GPUs, run time and getting software working are all words I use every day, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I deal with all five of these on my own jobs, so I can pick one from my last run without guessing.
screens.why4: The five are in my words and cover the real pains, but a job dying partway is what I was just asked about and has no direct option, and running out of allocation overlaps a little with waiting for a job to start, since both can show up as a long queue.
screens.why5: Guessing memory, GPUs and run time keeps the founder's situation in my trade's words and sits as one option among equals, with no product or company showing.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five short options I can hold, but the anchor plus the stem run a bit long and 'memory, GPUs and run time' is a list inside a list, which is a small mouthful when heard once.

screens.why1: After being asked about jobs failing and what I'd want made easier, asking how I sized my last job is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Sizing a job, padding it, and resubmitting are how I already talk about this work, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I size every job I submit, so I can answer from my last submission, even if it was a routine one.
screens.why4: These are recognisably my outcomes, but 'Copied an old script and hoped' describes a method with no result and overlaps the others, since a copied script can also be padded or die, and there is no option for over-requesting only slightly and still dying or for cases like a time-limit kill.
screens.why5: It stays on guessing resources before a submit, with nothing of a product or founder's terms reaching me.
screens.why6: Each option has a semicolon inside it while semicolons also separate the options, so heard once the list blurs into ten fragments, though the single short question itself says well.
screens.instead: Think of your last job submission. How did you set its resources? Options: From past runs, and it fit; Padded a little, some sat idle; Padded a lot, much sat idle; Set too low, and it died. Escape: I can't recall.
